There is a gap after the yes that almost nobody plans for, and in most companies it is about three weeks long. Sales has finished, delivery has not started, and for those three weeks nobody actually owns the customer. The cure is one sentence, and it has to be said before the end of the call where they agree: shall we lock in the kick-off date now, while everybody is still in the room. A date agreed in the room happens. A date agreed later by email is a date that slips, and it slips quietly. The other thing I watch, and this is the one that breaks plans, is any lead time that belongs to the customer. A firewall change, a purchase order, a security review. Twenty minutes of work and six weeks of waiting, and nothing in anybody's system will remind them it exists. So it goes on the plan on day one, with their name on it, said out loud.

I will tell you what I actually judge a supplier by, and it is not the demo and it is not the price. It is the first two weeks after I sign, because those two weeks tell me what the next two years are going to look like. The most common thing that happens, and the thing I remember longest, is that the salesperson disappears. Somebody new arrives, they ask me questions I already answered twice, and I understand that the person I was really dealing with was selling and not delivering. And there is one more thing I want in writing, even when it is bad news. Tell me the contingency, and tell me the lead times that belong to my own side. I would much rather see two weeks of contingency written down in March than discover it in June. A plan that hides that is a plan that is going to surprise me, and I have had enough surprises.
